articles.title_zh: AI Trade Stumbles After Tech Earnings, Oil Rallies: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
U.S. equity futures slid early Thursday after investors digested third-quarter earnings from Big Tech names including Meta Platforms and Tesla.
S&P 500 futures fell 0.66%, and Nasdaq-100 futures dropped 1.32%. Dow Jones Industrial Average futures ticked down 0.28%, or 147 points.
In Asia, markets traded lower. South Korea's Kospi fell more than 1%, while Japan's Nikkei 225 declined 0.73%. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 lost 0.53%. Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index is down more than 2%. Mainland China's CSI 300 is down 0.37%.
Shares of Meta gained 2% in extended trading. The Facebook and Instagram parent delivered a revenue beat along with strong guidance for the current quarter. Meanwhile, Tesla reported a better-than-expected top and bottom line for its third-quarter results. Shares of the electric vehicle maker were last off 3%.
"The quarter showed the AI investment paying off in the core," said Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives in his post Meta earnings reaction note. Spend is "better controlled than feared," Ives added as Meta narrowed the range for its full-year data center-related capital expenditures.
The action follows a positive day on Wall Street, with the S&P 500 notching a three-day win streak, while the Dow jumped 360 points. The Nasdaq Composite closed 1% higher, catching a tailwind from SpaceX and Tesla .
Blowout quarterly results from SpaceX fueled investors' excitement for the artificial intelligence trade, sending shares of Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices higher. Also fanning the flames was news from Super Micro Computer , which lifted its fiscal first-quarter revenue outlook .
There was also some focus on Nvidia's U.S. supply chain agreements Wednesday. The chip giant announced plans to expand global manufacturing capacity to meet growing demand for its accelerated computing and full-stack AI factory platform.
Looking ahead to Thursday, there are a host of companies on deck to report results including Procter & Gamble, Lockheed Martin, Valero Energy and Honeywell.
Investors will also be paying attention to the economic calendar with weekly initial jobless claims set to release Thursday morning.
French borrowing costs remained under pressure in morning European deals Thursday, with the yield on the 10-year OAT up nearly 6 basis points to 5.0514%.
The yield closed Wednesday around 5.02% , its highest level since 2002.
Mass protests and rioting over the weekend have further spooked investors , compounding existing concerns that the country's politicians will struggle to pass reforms to reduce the budget deficit and tackle its growing debt .
French stocks on the CAC 40 index were down 1.33% in early trade. Luxury goods giant Hermes fell 6.3% after missing analyst expectations for third-quarter revenues.
The pan-European Stoxx 600 was down 0.78% shortly after 8:10 a.m. in London (3:10 a.m. E.T.) as the continent's main bourses and sectors started Thursday's session mainly in the red.
Basic resources shed 2.22%, leading losses, as travel and leisure stocks slumped 1.94% in early dealmaking. Banks slipped 1.93% while technology names were down 1.79%.
Food and beverage stocks advanced more than 1%, while telecoms rose 0.39%, and oil and gas ticked 0.14% higher.
The French CAC 40 shed 0.82% in Paris, while Italy's FTSE MIB dropped 0.96% in Milan. In Frankfurt, Germany's DAX opened 0.73% lower, while in London, the U.K.'s FTSE 100 futures slipped 0.54%.
Nestlé CEO Philipp Navratil told CNBC Thursday that while third-quarter results were strong globally, the U.S. has been a tough market as shoppers face budget strains and seek value.
"Look, the U.S. numbers were also good in Q3... but consumers are still cautious, so it's not an easy environment in the U.S. at all," Navratil told CNBC's Carolin Roth on "Squawk Box Europe."
"Consumers look for value, they are stretched at the end of the month, and so we have to adapt the portfolio to the right price points," he said.
Nestlé reported organic sales growth of 4% in the third quarter, with real internal growth (volume and product mix) of 2.8%.
Nestlé's Americas sales improved in the third quarter, led by stronger U.S. and Latin American demand, despite continued weakness in some consumer segments.
"When we price, we do this with the aim to take consumers along...so we use different price points, different portfolio brands to really cater for each of the budgets out there," Navratil added.
Defense electronics group Thales boosted its full-year outlook early Thursday, amid a major rearmament push among European defense primes.
The company, best known for military radars, secure battlefield communications, and the sophisticated avionics and sensors it supplies for Dassault Aviation's Rafale fighter jet, said it now expects organic sales growth toward the upper end of its guided range of 6% to 7%, "and potentially beyond."
In the third quarter, organic sales grew 8.7% year-on-year to 5.5 billion euros ($6.2 billion). Order intake rose 3% to 6.7 billion euros as customers ordered its air defense radars and battlefield communications systems, driven by "sustained demand in most markets."
Thales also reported a sharp increase in orders from the Middle East regions, up 210% in the first 9 months of the year compared to the same period a year ago.
Barclays ' third quarter pre-tax profit came in at £2.3 billion ($3.1 billion), up 12% year-on-year, and in line with LSEG-compiled forecasts of £2.3 billion. Group income was £7.4 billion, compared to analysts' expected £7.61 billion.
Net interest income for the three-month period held steady at £3.91 billion, as the bank announced a new £500 million share buyback.
Barclays' CET1 capital ratio — a measure of a bank's solvency — was 14.2%, down from 14.3% at the end of the second quarter. Return on Tangible Equity, meanwhile, was 11.7%, versus 16.1% the previous quarter.
Stoxx 50 futures were more than 1% lower ahead of the market open, with European stock markets set to start Thursday's trading session in negative territory.
The French CAC 40 is set to open 0.91% lower, with Germany's DAX is seen starting down 0.73%. Italy's FTSE MIB was down about 1%.
In the U.K., FTSE 100 futures were off by 0.44%.
New car registrations in the European Union have risen 5.7% year to date, the European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA) said Thursday.
The industry group said the market was showing "notable resilience" despite headwinds including higher energy prices and volatile geopolitics.
Buyer support measures and a greater range of models on offer have meanwhile supported electric vehicle sales, ACEA said.
Hybrid-electric cars were the most popular, with 36.3% of the market. Battery-electric cars accounted for 22.7% of new EU registrations, while plug-in hybrid electric sales accounted for 10.1%.
The share of petrol and diesel cars fell from 36.9% to 28.2% year-on-year.
The Indian rupee has appreciated for eight straight sessions against the dollar, marking its longest strengthening streak since March 2025.
The rupee, which has been among the weakest Asian currencies for over a year, closed on Wednesday at a nearly four-month high of 94.46 rupees per dollar.
Devarsh Vakil, head of Prime Research at HDFC Securities, said the sustained momentum of the Indian currency has been "anchored by strategic central-bank intervention, healthy foreign inflows into the primary market and profit-taking in the US dollar."
Earlier this month, India's central bank announced measures that made it expensive to take speculative bets on the rupee and restricted rebooking of cancelled foreign exchange derivative contracts.  It also opened a special window to meet the entire daily dollar requirements of three public sector oil marketing companies, ring-fencing this trade from spot markets.

articles.title_orig: Meta Stock Split Deal Will Keep Mark Zuckerberg In California Amid Billionaire Tax Threat
articles.title_zh: Meta Stock Split Deal Will Keep Mark Zuckerberg In California Amid Billionaire Tax Threat
articles.content_orig:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg intends to maintain control over the company he founded in 2004 and a new class of stock will help him do just that.
On Wednesday as Meta released third quarter earnings results, the company announced that it would issue a new share class of Class C stock. The share class, which is technically a one-for-one stock dividend of new Class C shares, will be distributed to all shareholders. It was conceived following months of extensive negotiation that grew contentious at times between Zuckerberg and board members, including DoorDash CEO Tony Xu, Ambassador Robert Kimmitt, and ex- Microsoft executive Charles Songhurst. Xu disclosed his personal friendship with Zuckerberg but said it wouldn’t impair his judgement. At one point, the committee even talked about resigning if they couldn’t come to a resolution.
According to a Meta filing with the Securities & Exchange Commission, Zuckerberg wanted to be able to maintain his voting control, meet his pledges to fund the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative with his Meta stock, and be prepared to pay billions to the state of California if a proposed wealth tax is approved by voters in November.
The proposed wealth tax, however, came around the same time as a decision by the company in late 2025 that Meta needed to raise outside capital to help fund the AI boom. Zuckerberg holds about 60.6% of voting control at Meta, while his stake is about 13.4% of the company.
Like other major tech companies, Meta maintains a dual-class share structure, where Class A shares trade on Nasdaq as a one-vote-one-share stock. Conversely, Zuckerberg’s holdings are made up of mostly Class B shares, which carry 10 votes per share, which is how he maintains majority control. The condition on the supercharged Class B shares is if Zuckerberg sells them, they convert to Class A. Many companies require this condition for super-voting shares to ensure that outsiders don’t start to gain control of companies from founders seeking liquidity.
The rub is if Meta issues more Class A shares, which it does in order to make equity grants to employees, make acquisitions or raise capital, Zuckerberg’s stake gets diluted. Meta has long offset the dilution with stock buybacks, which helped buoy his voting power from 53.7% in 2013 to 60.6% now. But the buybacks also drain cash that Meta wants to use to fund the AI buildout. The company’s SEC filings show Meta repurchased $26.3 billion in Class A stock in 2025, but hasn’t bought back any shares in four straight quarters. Meanwhile, in the first nine months of this year, Meta posted $21 billion in stock-based compensation.
Meta’s third quarter results , released Wednesday, help explain why the share class came about. Revenue this quarter rose 26% to $64.6 billion while capital expenditures hit $34.9 billion. Meanwhile, free cash flow dipped to negative $2.1 billion, compared to $10.6 billion a year ago. Meta also forecast capex for 2026 at $135 billion to $140 billion, raising the low end up from $130 billion. Meta forecast fourth quarter revenue of $73 billion to $76 billion.
As a solution to the crunch, the new Class C stock will carry no votes, the company said. Meta will use them to pay employees, fund acquisitions, and raise capital without Zuckerberg losing majority voting control. He can also sell some of them without giving up votes, and more importantly, pay a potentially massive wealth tax bill looming in California without having to tap into his Class B shares. His current level of control is such that he can personally elect all the directors on the board and determine most of the issues proposed to shareholders for a vote, which won’t change following the recapitalization. With the new shares, Zuckerberg can sell 20% right away, and the remaining 80% are “stapled”—meaning he can sell them only if he sells or converts an equal number of his voting shares.
Proposition 40 in California, known as the wealth tax, is up for a vote on Nov. 3 and if it passes, it could hit Zuckerberg and the wealthiest in the state with a multibillion bill. The Bloomberg Billionaires index lists him at #5 with a net worth of $246 billion. In July, Zuckerberg told Kimmitt, who is Meta’s lead independent director, that selling his Class B stock to cover what he might owe for the wealth tax could cut his voting stake back down to 53%.
The tax came up in a conversation between the two after negotiations between Zuckerberg and the committee appeared to grow tense. The committee had suggested shareholder-friendly sunset provisions that would see the Class B shares convert into regular stock within a year of Zuckerberg’s eventual death or departure from Meta—or if he sold more than half his holdings. During a call with Kimmitt in July, the two discussed the wealth tax and noted that Zuckerberg had only taken a $1 salary from Meta since 2013.
Later that same month, Zuckerberg again brought up Prop 40, this time raising concerns about whether it might impact his ability to stay a California resident. The following week, Zuckerberg’s lawyers sent a letter asking for a pay package similar to those made to other tech founders, partly so Zuckerberg could pay a potential tax bill. Like SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk, many founders in tech have moonshot performance pay packages, in which rigorous stock price growth is tied to massive pay hurdles. According to the filing, Zuckerberg refused to consider any changes to his voting shares, including sunset provisions, and told the committee he was “considering establishing residence outside of California.”
The next day, the committee hashed over Zuckerberg’s stance and went over Meta’s analyst coverage and commentary, and the tightening of credit conditions for hyperscalers. Meta had seen  relatively looser demand for its July bond issuance for a Texas data center. The committee wanted to keep Zuckerberg in California, close to its artificial intelligence lab.
Later that same day, August 4, Zuckerberg proposed a dividend of 20 shares of Class C stock for each share of Class A and B shares, paid to all shareholders. He told the committee he wouldn’t agree to sunsetting his Class Bs or support equity financing that diluted his voting control.
Then, he upped the stakes.
Zuckerberg told the committee “he intended to establish residence outside California, which he had been advised he would need to do before the November. 3, 2026 election,” the filing states.
The committee met again August 5, but viewed the 20-for-1 proposal as “excessive,” the filing states. By late August, all sides were dug in after various proposals had been issued and objected to. Eventually, committee members discussed dissolving the committee or resigning from the board if Zuckerberg wouldn’t make concessions for the benefit of all Class A shareholders.
At a September 9 board dinner, Zuckerberg told directors he planned to list his Palo Alto estate for sale on September 13. Committee members had recused themselves from dinner during his update. And then within days, a new proposal came together. Zuckerberg dropped his pay request and agreed to keep the $1 salary and committed to stay in California or wherever Meta is headquartered, for eight years. All shareholders get another one-for-one Class C dividend every time the stock price doubles from $580.60, so long as annual returns are at least 10%.
The deal was inked on September 14. Every Class A and Class B share will get one Class C share, effectively a two-for-one split and Zuckerberg can sell 20% of his new Class C shares right away. The committee approved days before the full board sealed the deal on October 19. Chan Zuckerberg entities that hold 56% of the vote signed off the following day and the new shares take effect on Jan. 19, 2027.
Chief financial officer Susan Li said Wednesday trading of the Class C stock will begin in late January. She said Meta has no specific financing plans yet.

Sea mines have resurfaced as a threat in the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran claimed Oct.17 that two oil tankers caught fire after striking the explosives, raising fresh alarms over the safety of one of the world's most critical shipping lanes.
This came as the International Maritime Organization (IMO) warned that sea mines pose a serious threat to vessels navigating the strategic waterway and while Tehran continues to maintain its own unauthorized shipping corridor inside its territorial waters.
"The traffic separation scheme, the information that we have is that they still have mines. And of course, whilst the conflict is ongoing, it's very difficult for us to use third parties to verify that it is clear of these hazards," IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez told Fox News Digital.

"So in the meantime, we cannot guarantee that a vessel that intends to transit that route will not be hit by a mine."
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) navy said Saturday that two oil tankers caught fire after striking naval mines while crossing the Strait of Hormuz, Reuters reported, citing Iran's official Islamic Republic News Agency (IRNA).
State media also said both tankers were carrying about 2 million barrels of crude oil, according to Reuters .
IRNA also reported that the vessels had switched off their positioning and radar systems and attempted to use a route through the strategic waterway that Iran had not authorized.

The alleged strikes came as Tehran continued to maintain its transit passageway inside Iranian territorial waters, imposing tolls and safety fees administered by the IRGC — a framework rejected by Washington and the IMO as inconsistent with international maritime law.
International shipping through the narrow chokepoint has historically relied on an IMO-approved traffic separation scheme adopted in 1968.
"Right now there's only one route that was adopted back in 1968 that is approved and recognized for IMO and that appears in all the charts for the vessels to operate," Dominguez explained.

"Any other route needs to actually be sent to the organization to go through the processes, and we have not received that."
"We have received communication from Iran to use that route because of the conflict," Dominguez clarified.

The Strait of Hormuz is "not open for business in the way that it was before the conflict started," he said.

articles.title_orig: U.S. pulls diplomats from Saudi Arabia as it reportedly readies Iran strikes after midterms
articles.title_zh: U.S. pulls diplomats from Saudi Arabia as it reportedly readies Iran strikes after midterms
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. ordered non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks on the kingdom escalate.
The move comes as the U.S. and Israeli militaries have drawn up specific plans for renewed strikes on Iran after next month's midterm elections, according to The New York Times, citing unnamed U.S. officials.
Planning for a "short but intensive" operation is progressing, The Times said.
The developments point to a possible widening of the nearly eight-month war, while U.S. and Iranian negotiators continue talks on Tehran's nuclear program and the Strait of Hormuz.
State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott in a post on X said the order applies only to Saudi Arabia, citing increasing attacks by Iran-aligned Houthis on civilian targets. Meanwhile, Reuters reported Washington also plans to withdraw family members from other missions in the region.
A strike Wednesday on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam killed at least one person and injured eight. Two people died in a drone attack on Saudi Aramco's Shaybah oil field, the Saudi Press Agency reported, adding that operations were not affected.
In recent days, the U.S. and Israeli militaries have stepped up military exercises, including flying planes over Iraq to practice strike maneuvers, according to The New York Times. The Times also reported that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during an unannounced visit to Israel this week to discuss potential new strikes.
The renewed military strikes would likely target Iran's energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and missile and drone arsenal, according to The Times, noting that President Donald Trump has yet to approve the fresh strikes and has repeatedly vetoed plans for a return to major combat this year.
Iranian officials have vowed to widen their attacks to target data centers and undersea internet cables, while refusing concessions on their nuclear program.
Despite the persistent shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, Middle East oil flows through the vital strait have recovered to near pre‑war levels according to Kpler.
As Brent crude topped $110 a barrel and West Texas Intermediate gained 1% to $98.12, recovering appetite for crude from China could drive oil prices higher, according to the commodity research firm.
"China's crude import demand is expected to continue recovering, driven by rising refinery throughput and rapidly declining crude inventories," said Muyu Xu, senior crude oil analyst at Kpler. The war has cut China's oil stockpiles, with the fastest drawndown on record at 1.6 million barrels a day in September, Xu estimated.
China still holds 1.1 billion barrels in reserves, about 80 days of refinery needs, Xu said. She added that with virtually all Iranian cargoes outside the U.S. blockade discharged, substantial new crude arrivals in China appear unlikely.
Chinese state-owned refiners are likely to have a stronger appetite and greater urgency to secure prompt Middle Eastern barrels as they face higher throughput and inventory-replenishment needs. Independent refiners are also seeking alternatives to Iranian crude, a shift that could limit further downside in the Dubai structure, Xu said.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: Musk’s public endorsement of SpaceX-Tesla deal may throw a wrench in talks
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Musk’s public endorsement of SpaceX-Tesla deal may throw a wrench in talks
articles.content_orig:
Elon Musk has spent years building Tesla and SpaceX into a pair of trillion-dollar technology empires. Now, he is considering bringing them together .
Asked on Tuesday whether a merger would be a good idea, Musk was clear: "Yes."
The prospect is more than hypothetical. Musk said special committees have been formed to assess a potential deal, although he stressed that there is no guarantee a merger will happen and that nothing has been agreed.
With Tesla valued at roughly $1.5 trillion (£1.1 trillion) and SpaceX at $2 trillion, a combination of the two companies would mark the largest merger ever.
Any deal would also need shareholder backing. But Musk said he saw "a lot to be gained" in bringing the businesses together.
"In my opinion, 100%. It's just a question of when," says David Nicholson, chief technology advisor at market research firm The Futurum Group.
During Tesla's earnings call on Wednesday, Musk said he had nothing further to add about the prospect of a merger but quipped: "I feel like I'm tap-dancing through a minefield."
Musk said that calling the merger a certainty would be "overstating" things.
Tesla reported a slight drop in third quarter sales which came in at $28.05 billion compared with $28.1 billion at the same time last year.
The unveiling of the Tesla Roadster last week - a futuristic electric car powered by SpaceX rocket thrusters - served as a "symbolic embodiment" hinting at the two Musk companies merging, Nicholson said.
Musk, chief executive of both SpaceX and Tesla, said bringing the firms together would be beneficial given the work each does around chips, artificial intelligence (AI) and other technology projects.
Specifically, the deal would combine Tesla's cars, robots and self-driving technology with SpaceX's rockets, data centres, satellites and telecommunications operations.
The move could be a step towards Musk's mission to build a self-sustaining city on Mars - a vision that has invited sceptics but also plenty of backers.
Over the past year, Musk has moved to consolidate his businesses, with SpaceX acquiring xAI and X, formerly Twitter, before going public this year.
But the merger would ultimately be decided by shareholders, with half of Tesla's needed to back the deal, a threshold even Musk described as "quite a high hurdle".
Musk, as boss of both companies, cannot participate in shareholder discussions.
Even so, Musk, a key shareholder of Tesla, will likely get his way in the next few years, said investment analyst Dan Sheehan from Telos Wealth Advisors.
He believes shareholders will back the deal as the technology the companies develop complement each other, Sheehan said.
But the merger would mean that Tesla shareholders will likely hold a "smaller slice of a much larger and more complex business," he added.
"There's no real precedent for how a public company like Tesla gets priced in this," Sheehan said.
SpaceX shares rose 8% in after hours trading while shares of Tesla climbed by 2%.
Experts told the BBC that Tesla drivers are unlikely to see much drastic change in the near term, even if the two companies combine.
In fact, vehicles seem almost like "an afterthought", overshadowed by the potential to combine the Tesla and SpaceX's tech capabilities, Nicholson said.
Changes are already underway at Tesla. The carmaker said earlier this year that it would prioritise its best-selling Model Y and Model 3, shifting focus away from less popular models .
Tesla also started using a manufacturing plant in California to produce humanoid robots, known as Optimus.
Pairing Tesla's self-driving technology and robotics with SpaceX's AI and satellite network could result in more capable vehicles, Sheehan said.
"The question is how much priority cars get inside a company increasingly driven by AI infrastructure," he added.
The recent Roadster showcase suggests SpaceX technology could be pulled into future Tesla products, which could attract more customers, said Tu Le, the founder of advisory firm Sino Auto Insights.
The Cybertruck-maker faces intense competition from Chinese carmakers like BYD, which overtook Tesla as the world's biggest EV maker in January.
The biggest winner is probably Musk - the world's richest man who also became the world's first trillionaire earlier this year.
The merger would give Musk greater voting control over the combined company than he currently has at Tesla, a factor the special committee assessing the deal would have to consider.
A single company makes it easier for Musk to run his AI strategy the way he wants, Sheehan said.
"The deal itself doesn't add to Musk's wealth, but it concentrates it further in one stock," he said.
However, the merger could attract scrutiny over Musk, already a polarising figure in the US, Nicholson said.
The move could also face more regulatory pressure if Democrats - many of whom have been critical of Musk - win more seats in the US midterm elections next month.
Shareholders have backed Musk's desires before. Last year, Tesla investors approved an unprecedented compensation package for Musk valued around $1tn .
"I honestly don't think Musk will be keeping track of what the merger will do for his wealth," Nicholson said.
The deal also brings Musk closer to what Nicholson says is "his mission in life": colonising Mars.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine’s strikes on Russian data centers disrupt key services and derail AI research
articles.title_zh: Ukraine’s strikes on Russian data centers disrupt key services and derail AI research
articles.content_orig:
From accessing their money to ordering a taxi or takeout, millions of Russians were feeling the impact of Ukrainian strikes on the data centers of the country’s internet giant Yandex in their daily life.
“I ended up in a situation where I had absolutely no money. Well, I had the money, but it was inaccessible,” said Irina, a blogger from St. Petersburg, who had not been able to access her money for four days when she spoke with NBC News last week.
Irina, who like several other people did not want her last name shared while she was speaking with a foreign news organization about a sensitive matter, said her rent was due the day the first outages happened, when she hoped “that it would be fixed in a few hours.” Days later, she still had no access to money to pay for utilities or even food for her small child.
The strikes that took place over several days this month were the first publicized attacks on Russian data centers as Ukraine seeks to bring the war home for Russians .
The disruption hit myriad services provided by Yandex, a tech giant akin to Google whose services are deeply integrated into daily life in Russia and whose digital infrastructure other third-party platforms rely on.
Many people took to social media to complain about not being able to order taxis or food delivery. Others reported not being able to access their files on the company’s storage service, while some even struggled to get into their homes after their digital keys went offline.
While most Yandex services have been coming back online, three people told NBC News they had been left locked out of their disposable cash and savings for days after disruptions to Yandex Pay, a digital payment service that many Russians use.
Irina, 21, said that in the future she will diversify her deposits across different banks and have a “substantial cash reserve” just in case.
Yandex said Oct. 9 that no employees were hurt and that it is working to restore service.
“Data centers are the iron heart of Yandex,” the statement said. “Their operation is critical for services that have become part of people’s everyday lives.”
Anastasiya Mityaeva, 25, who splits her time between Moscow and the southern city of Krasnodar, said she was “shocked” by the outages, which initially left her family worried about being able to pay down their mortgage after her account, her mother’s account and her grandmother’s account were all inaccessible.
“The uncertainty was scary,” said Mityaeva, who has 2 million followers on TikTok and is originally from Russian-annexed Crimea. “We realized just how much hangs on Yandex. We did not quite appreciate it before.”
Mityaeva, who regained access to her money after several days, also had issues calling a taxi on the first day of the outages and encountered problems with the system to enter her apartment building. Her Yandex home voice assistant, equivalent to an Amazon Echo, stopped responding to requests to play music and turn off the lights.
She did not blame the company, saying Yandex was a “hostage of the situation,” adding: “I understand that this was not up to them. This came from the outside.”
Others were more critical of the company. Viktoria, 30, a barista from Moscow, said she plans to stop using Yandex completely after she was unable to access her money during the outages, describing it as the last straw after other recent issues.
She said Saturday that she once again had access to her money through Yandex Pay but that the service was displaying the wrong balance on her account.
Three taxi drivers in Moscow, who use Yandex’s taxi application to take orders and get paid, all told NBC News they could not see how much money they were making and could not withdraw their earnings during the outage. One of the drivers said he has stopped working altogether until the problem gets fixed. He is originally from Kyrgyzstan and did not know why the outages were happening.
Another driver, Valery from Krasnodar, had been on the job for only a few months, having previously worked at a packing center for Wildberries, Russia’s retail giant, whose warehouse was attacked by Ukrainian drones in July .
When the Yandex outages started, he said, the taxi app would show error messages or even send several cars for the same customer.
While that has been largely resolved, said Valery, 24, the biggest issue for him was that he could not withdraw the money that he had already earned with Yandex. “If I can’t access my pay in another week or two, I will start looking for another job,” he said.
In addition to Yandex, the data centers of Russia’s biggest bank, Sberbank, and the tech giant VK have also been targeted in recent days.
The chaos is no accident, analysts say. “Ukraine’s campaign from the start has had as one of its objectives bringing home to ordinary Russians the fact that they are at war and this involves consequences,” Keir Giles, an associate fellow at Chatham House, a British think tank, told NBC News.
The aim, Giles said, is for everyday Russians to conclude that their lives are being disrupted because of their leaders’ actions in waging war.
Yandex may also be a target because of its role in shaping what Russians see online, said Robert Tollast, a drone expert and researcher at the Royal United Services Institute in London.
Data centers also have growing military value, Tollast said, as both sides use battlefield data to improve operations and commanders’ situational awareness, potentially with AI-assisted planning.
Asked about the outages and whether the government was looking into financially assisting those affected, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said it was premature to talk about government support, because Yandex is “facing difficulties,” but it is “strong and powerful.” Meanwhile, Russian authorities were looking at protecting data centers after the “unprecedented attack,” Digital Development Minister Maksut Shadayev said.
On Wednesday, President Vladimir Putin held a meeting on enhancing the level of digital security in Russia, but Peskov said it was not linked to the attacks on data centers.
Russia has increasingly ramped up its own attacks on Ukrainian data centers, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy accusing Moscow of trying to “leave Ukrainians without the internet.” Ukraine was reciprocating those strikes by hitting Yandex, he said in a speech last week, adding without providing evidence that “it suddenly became a little easier to breathe on many social media platforms” because there were fewer Russian bots around. NBC News could not verify whether Yandex services’ going down had that effect.
While both sides have hit data centers, Russia’s were easier targets, said Mykhailo Samus, a Ukrainian military analyst and director of the New Geopolitics Research Network.
While Ukraine’s data centers are widely dispersed, many of Russia’s are concentrated in a handful of large facilities, he said, meaning a strike on a single site can disrupt services spanning transportation, internet access and payments.
“Very easy and very important,” he said.
Yuliya Talmazan is a reporter for NBC News Digital, based in London.

articles.title_orig: China's stock market sinks into bear territory as CSI 300 extends 10-week rout
articles.title_zh: China's stock market sinks into bear territory as CSI 300 extends 10-week rout
articles.content_orig:
China's benchmark CSI 300 index on Thursday entered bear-market territory, falling 20% from its June peak, as a prolonged sell-off in its equities deepens.
The index, which tracks 300 of the largest stocks listed in Shanghai and Shenzhen, has declined for 10 consecutive weeks and is down 2.6% so far this week, underscoring sustained pressure on Chinese equities, data from LSEG showed. The index was more than 1% lower Thursday.
Jordan Cvetanovski, chairman and CIO at Pella Funds, said China's equity market continues to face structural challenges, particularly as the world's second-largest economy grapples with the fallout from years of excess capacity and overinvestment.
"I think China is really struggling with reining in the problems that they've had in the past from the overbuild of capacity and other things," Cvetanovski told CNBC, pointing to challenges facing companies even in globally competitive industries such as batteries — a sector where he still sees select opportunities in China.
Chinese firms have been suffering from declining profit growth amid intense competition that has eroded margins and even invited the government to step in. In September, the country posted it's weakest growth in industrial profits this year.
The world's second-largest economy also posted its slowest growth in over three years in the second quarter, pressured by a multiyear slowdown in the property sector and extended weakness in consumer demand.
Shaun Rein, managing director at China Market Research Group, expects further selling pressure as geopolitical uncertainty, concerns over an artificial intelligence bubble and deteriorating consumer confidence weigh on investor sentiment.
China's large base of retail investors could also exacerbate market volatility, Rein said, as individual investors are prone to exiting the market faster during periods of uncertainty.
Unlike major markets such as the New York Stock Exchange, where retail investors account for about 20%-25% of trade volumes, China's retail investors drive 90% of daily trading, according to data provided by HSBC.
"For Chinese, it's about wealth preservation," Rein said, noting that investors are increasingly favoring safer assets such as time deposits amid a weakening property market and sluggish labor conditions.
While Rein expects increased pressure on markets, he said the sell-off has been excessive, pointing to resilient exports and signs of a recovery in property prices in China's largest cities.
"It's a crisis of confidence right now not a crisis in the economy," he said, predicting a strong rebound in Chinese equities in 2027.
Daniel Gerard, senior multi-asset strategist at State Street Markets, also struck a more optimistic tone, saying that China's growing capabilities in artificial intelligence could eventually draw global investors back into its equity market, even before corporate earnings recover.

articles.title_orig: Tests show Pope Leo XIV won’t need further treatment for lung cancer, Vatican says
articles.title_zh: Tests show Pope Leo XIV won’t need further treatment for lung cancer, Vatican says
articles.content_orig:
Pope Leo XIV’s lung cancer surgery last week was a success, and no further treatment is required, the Vatican press office said in a bulletin Wednesday.
“The final histological reports and molecular biology analyses of the tissue removed during the Holy Father’s surgery have been completed today,” said Dr. Luigi Carbone, the pope’s personal physician, and Dr. Stefano Margaritora, a thoracic surgery professor who led the surgical team.
“The results have confirmed that the condition was a pulmonary adenocarcinoma and that the disease was localized. A subsequent oncological evaluation has confirmed that no further therapy is required,” the bulletin added.
Pulmonary adenocarcinoma is the most common type of lung cancer, accounting for roughly 40% of all cases. It’s slow-moving and often affects nonsmokers.
Leo’s announcement on October 11 that he required surgery for a “nodule” on his lung came as a shock both within and outside the Vatican, given the pope’s penchant for clean living. After a short stay at a hospital in Rome, where doctors removed the lobe of his left lung, Leo returned home on October 17.
The next day, he made his first public appearance since his diagnosis, leading the Sunday Angelus from the balcony of the Apostolic Palace.
“This experience has given me a profound sense of closeness to all those who are going through illness or a state of infirmity,” he told crowds of worshipers.
Pope Leo’s recovery has beeen much faster than normal, according to Dr. Juanita Mora, the national medical spokesperson for the American Lung Association, who was not part of his care team. She said doctors will monitor the pope after his recent treatment, including follow-up CT scans every three to six months for the first few years, then annually to check for any regrowth.
After such surgery, patients often have respiratory physiotherapy to restore breathing capacity, Mora told CNN, adding that his affected lung should regain full function.
The all-clear arrives ahead of the pontiff’s planned South America trip next month. The news that the pope had cancer complicated plans for the journey, scheduled to include stops in Peru, Uruguay and Argentina and require at least 14 flights.
Though the Vatican has not officially confirmed the pope’s plans for travel, Margaritora, his surgeon, told Vatican News that he saw “no clinical reasons” for canceling the trip.
If the trip goes ahead, the pontiff will probably be told to walk during his travels to prevent blood clots that can form during long flights, according to Mora. The pope, she said, should get Covid-19, flu and RSV vaccines ahead of his trip for “a little extra protection in case he were to get any of the respiratory infections.”
CNN’s Sharon Braithwaite and Jen Christensen contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Hackers Exploited the PHP Vulnerabilities Days Before They Were Patched
articles.title_zh: Hackers Exploited the PHP Vulnerabilities Days Before They Were Patched
articles.content_orig:
The internet’s mad scramble on Wednesday to patch a pair of critical vulnerabilities in PHP , a widely used web scripting language, was already too late to stop every attack, newly released details reveal.
Wednesday’s release of fixes for two critical vulnerabilities in PHP caused administrators and security staff to race to identify and patch vulnerable websites and apps, while attackers inevitably reverse engineered the fixes to learn how to exploit the flaws. Some governments and other groups even proactively took key websites down in anticipation of the release, so they wouldn't be targeted before they could apply the patches.
But in addition to detecting such active exploitation on Wednesday, research published Wednesday evening by Amazon Web Services indicates that at least one actor had started attempting to exploit the bugs—known collectively as PHP2Shell—on October 17, four days before Wednesday's public revelations.
AWS analysts spotted the October 17 exploitation on Wednesday while looking back at activity on one of their so-called honeypots, or intentionally vulnerable web servers or other digital lures that help researchers study attack methods and trends. The attempt came from an IP address that AWS says is linked to a “commercial anonymization network,” in other words a proxy network or VPN .
“While the vulnerability was under embargo, the targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure,” CJ Moses, AWS's chief information security officer, wrote in the research post.
Proof-of-concept exploits for PHP2Shell began emerging publicly on Wednesday, with some seeming to appear hours before the public disclosure at 10 am ET. In the hours leading up to the disclosure, AWS researchers say their honeypots were hit with multiple exploitation attempts anonymized using various providers and seemingly with various attack goals, likely indicating multiple different actors. “Technical analysis is ongoing, and it’s unclear if any of these attempts would have succeeded in real-world systems,” Moses wrote. He added that “PHP2Shell is now being broadly exploited in the wild.”
The PHP Foundation did not immediately respond to WIRED's request for comment.
Though it is unclear how the exploitation on October 17 happened or where it came from, AWS emphasizes that the findings underscore how coordinated vulnerability disclosure must evolve and speed up, given global access to AI tools that can accelerate vulnerability analysis and allow less technically proficient actors to quickly develop new exploits.
“The time from patch to working exploit is shrinking for structural reasons,” Moses wrote. “In the past, most exploitation we observed came after a public proof of concept was released. A small number of capable actors built exploits, and everyone else waited for them. That dependency is weakening. AI-assisted analysis makes it cheaper to turn a patch diff or advisory into a working exploit. As a result, more actors can act within hours or even minutes once technical details of a vulnerability are disclosed.”

articles.title_orig: North Korea says it will resume propaganda broadcasts across border into South Korea
articles.title_zh: North Korea says it will resume propaganda broadcasts across border into South Korea
articles.content_orig:
FILE - A soldier stands at a North Korean military guard post next to loudspeakers, seen from Paju, South Korea, near the border with North Korea, on Feb. 26, 2026. Ahn Young-joon/AP hide caption
SEOUL, South Korea — North Korea plans to resume anti-Seoul propaganda broadcasts along the heavily armed border with South Korea, leader Kim Jong Un's sister said, reviving a psychological warfare campaign as tensions rise after land mine blasts injured three South Korean front-line soldiers.
Kim Yo Jong, her brother's top spokesperson on Washington and Seoul, made the announcement Wednesday after visiting front-line areas where North Korean troops are reinforcing the border. She renewed a threat to retaliate against any South Korean provocation aimed at the fortification work.
In a follow-up statement Thursday, she said the North would place "new counter means" on alert along the border and have its loudspeakers on "standby" within days.
North Korea has been adding mines, barbed wire fences, anti-tank barriers and other fortifications to what's already one of the world's most heavily armed borders as Kim Jong Un pushes a hard line toward Seoul.
Touring the area with Marshal Pak Jong Chon, one of her brother's top military officials, Kim Yo Jong called the fortification work a "sacred and great undertaking" supporting the leader's policy of permanently severing ties with South Korea, which he has declared his most hostile adversary amid a broader diplomatic stalemate with Washington.
In this photo provided Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026, by the North Korean government, Kim Yo Jong, center left, sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, visits frontline areas, with military officials, in North Korea Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026. Independent journalists were not given access to cover the event depicted in this image distributed by the North Korean government. The content of this image is as provided and cannot be independently verified. KCNA via KNS/via AP hide caption
"Our tactical hunting teams are taking new positions, and within October, the loudspeakers for psychological warfare against the ROK will be in operation along the whole border," Kim Yo Jong said, using the initials of South Korea's formal name, the Republic of Korea.
She warned that if South Korean warning shots — which Seoul says are meant to force North Korean soldiers doing fortification work back across the border — cause "actual harm to our territorial security and our service persons' safety," North Korean border guards "will show no mercy for the armed gangsters bereft of reason."
Asked about Kim Yo Jong's threat to resume the loudspeaker broadcasts, South Korean Defense Ministry spokesperson Chung Binna said Thursday that Seoul would need to take "proportionate measures" in response to the North's moves along the border, but did not elaborate on what steps are being considered.
North Korea's state-run Korean Central News Agency first reported Kim's border visit as Tuesday, but Kim later corrected it to early Wednesday in a separate statement.
Following an inspection with the U.S.-led United Nations Command, Seoul formally blamed North Korean-planted mines for the Sept. 21 border blasts and urged the North to apologize and clear its remaining mines. North Korea denied responsibility for the explosions and warned of strong retaliation if provoked.
"Our military leadership underlined the need to make those rogues aware that our new firepower units have taken their firing positions," Kim told soldiers during her visit Wednesday, reminding them of her brother's order to make the border with the "enemy ... eternally impregnable."
South Korea's military has said North Korean soldiers crossed the border's military demarcation line 50 times this year during fortification work, and that it responded with warning shots and broadcasts. Kim has said South Korean's claims of border crossings are a "false pretext," and that its provocations have increased "beyond the red line" since the mine blasts.
South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff chairman, Jin Yong-Sung, called Kim's threats "intolerable" and ordered the military to "sternly respond" to potential provocations by the North.
During Tuesday's border inspection, Pak accused the South of making "deliberate, premeditated and absurd" claims to shift blame over the rising tensions and threatened an "overwhelming response" to South Korean provocations. He also denied that the North Korean soldiers were breaching the border during fortification work, saying "our army knows where our borderline is better than any others," KCNA said.
Loudspeaker broadcasts are among the Cold War-era psychological warfare tactics the two Koreas have occasionally used against each other during times of tensions.
South Korea's liberal government, led by President Lee Jae Myung, halted its broadcasts after taking office last year to improve ties with the North, which later stopped its own.
Kim Jong Un in recent years has cut off all diplomacy and cooperation with South Korea and declared it a permanent enemy as a yearslong stalemate in nuclear negotiations with Washington drags on.

articles.title_zh: Asian stocks sink to 3-month low on tech angst, Gulf tensions
articles.content_orig:
Get the best experience and stay connected to your community with our Spectrum News app. Learn More
NEW YORK (AP) — The U.S. stock market rose Wednesday following strong profit reports from SpaceX , Capital One Financial and other big companies.
The S&P 500 added 0.6% and pulled within 0.8% of its all-time high set earlier this month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 360 points, or 0.7%, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 1.1%.
SpaceX helped lead the market and climbed 7.8% after reporting a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected. Elon Musk, who runs the company that makes money from artificial-intelligence technology, rockets and other businesses, also said that SpaceX took a step to consider a possible merger with Tesla, his electric-vehicle company.
Tesla rose 3.4% and was one of the strongest forces lifting the S&P 500.
Other stocks rallying on profit reports that topped analysts’ expectations included Capital One Financial, which rose 2.5%, and Winnebago Industries, which climbed 10.7%.
Expectations are high for profit growth for all kinds of companies during the summer, and they need to meet them to justify the big runs their stock prices have made despite worries about high inflation , higher interest rates and other challenges weighing on Wall Street.
Winnebago was able to report a more resilient profit than expected even as high fuel prices and frustration among U.S. shoppers restrain interest in recreational vehicles, for example. CEO Michael Happe said its more expensive towable RVs are a tougher sell, but customers are interested in its “more accessible” offerings.
On the losing side of Wall Street was Netflix , which fell 5.3% even though the streaming service reported a stronger profit than analysts expected. Investors focused instead on worries that Netflix’s momentum may be slowing. The company’s forecast for revenue growth in the final three months of the year fell short of analysts’ expectations.
AT&T fell 6.4% even though it likewise delivered a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It gave a forecast for growth this year in an underlying measure of earnings before income taxes and some other things that fell short of some analysts’ expectations.
Among AI stocks, which have been at the center of the market’s action in recent weeks, the movements remained unsettled.
After leading the rest of the market for years because of the frenzy around AI, stocks in the industry have become shaky on worries that the build out of data centers may slow because of how much more expensive it’s become to borrow money.
CoreWeave, which has borrowed money to buy AI chips that it rents out to customers over the cloud, has been particularly volatile. Its stock bounced between an early gain of nearly 4% and a drop of 4.5% Wednesday morning before finishing with a dip of 0.5%. A day earlier, it careened between a gain of 5% and a drop of more than 6%.
Other AI-linked stocks were more resilient, and Nvidia’s rise of 2.5% was the strongest force lifting the S&P 500.
Besides SpaceX’s profit report showing strength for AI spending, another encouraging signal for the industry came from Super Micro Computer, which sells AI servers and services. It said it expects to report stronger revenue for the summer than it had earlier forecast because of “increased demand for AI platforms,” and its stock rallied 9.5%.
All told, the S&P 500 rose 44.60 points to 7,757.17. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 360.21 to 52,856.09, and the Nasdaq composite climbed 278.04 to 26,702.86.
In the bond market, the yield on the 10-year Treasury erased an early dip and climbed back to 5.12%, where it was late Tuesday.
It swung with oil prices, which remained unsteady. The price for a barrel of Brent crude drifted between $108 and $111 before settling at $108.82.
It’s been yo-yoing between $97 and $112 through October on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow the global energy industry to return to normal.
In stock markets abroad, indexes rose in Europe following a mixed finish in Asia. South Korea’s Kospi jumped 3.3% for one of the world’s biggest moves as AI stocks regained strength.

articles.title_orig: Australian Zoo Plays Matchmaker for Giant Birds, and Big Green Eggs Are Proof
articles.title_zh: Australian Zoo Plays Matchmaker for Giant Birds, and Big Green Eggs Are Proof
articles.content_orig:
Adelaide Zoo recorded its first Southern Cassowary egg in 34 years.
Ten-year-old Martina laid the bright green egg after being paired with 13-year-old Jeffrey.
The egg's fertility is unknown, and incubation takes about 50 days.
Adelaide Zoo in Australia celebrated the arrival of its first cassowary eggs in decades.
Two cassowary eggs were laid over the last few days, according to the zoo's Facebook page.
The milestone comes after caretakers carefully paired the zoo's female cassowary, 10-year-old Martina, with its 13-year-old male, Jeffrey, for the first time.
FILE - One of two cassowary eggs that were laid at Adelaide Zoo. (Zoos SA via Storyful)
Zoo employees have yet to confirm whether the eggs are even fertilized, but the fact that the eggs were laid at all is still a huge success for the species, according to a zoo news release.
"This is really exciting news for us because it has been 34 years since we've had successful cassowary chicks here at Adelaide Zoo, so the team and myself included are very excited," Team Supervisor Birds and Free Flight, Erin, said.
Since it is unclear whether the eggs have been fertilized, caretakers will be monitoring the nesting area and the birds' behavior closely in the meantime.
Cassowary can lay a clutch of between three and five eggs, according to the zoo.
It takes about 50 days to incubate and typically the male cassowary cares for and raises the chicks.
The bright green color of the shell helps camouflage the eggs from predators, according to the zoo.

In both polls, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party came in second, trailing Yashar and falling to 19 seats.
Neither poll found that either of the political blocs would win a clear majority; however, the opposition bloc continued to lead Netanyahu's.
N12 projected that the opposition bloc would win 55 seats and Netanyahu's bloc 51. By comparison, the Channel 13 poll showed Eisenkot's bloc gaining one seat to 52, while Netanyahu's bloc lost one seat to 49.
Whether Ofer Winter's People of Israel party and Yoaz Hendel and Yaron Zelekha's Reservists-Economic Party cross the 3.25% electoral threshold could affect the balance between the political blocs in the upcoming elections.
Former prime minister Naftali Bennett's B'Yachad party remained unchanged at 14 seats, while the Democrats, led by Yair Golan, gained one seat to reach 10, Channel 13 found. In N12, the Democrats remained at nine seats, while B'Yachad gained one seat to reach 15, its highest showing in a month and a half.
In both polls, Avigdor Liberman's Yisrael Beytenu polled at eight seats, and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir's Otzma Yehudit received seven.
Shas, led by Arye Deri, received eight seats in the N12 poll but seven on Channel 13, while United Torah Judaism, led by Yakov Asher, received seven in the N12 poll but eight on Channel 13.
The Religious Zionist Party (RZP) and Zehut, led by Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich and Moshe Feiglin, received six seats in the N12 poll, which rose to eight in the Channel 13 poll.
The Joint List , comprising Hadash, Ta'al, and Balad and led by Yousef Jabareen, received nine seats in both polls; however, N12 found that Mansour Abbas's Ra'am was polling at five, while Channel 13 placed Ra'am at 6. In both polls, the Arab parties remained stable, earning the same number of seats as in the previous poll.
In the N12 poll, the People of Israel party won four seats, crossing the electoral threshold after falling below it in the previous two polls. However, the Reservists-Economic Party remained below the electoral threshold with 2.8% of the vote.
In contrast, the Channel 13 poll reversed the two. The Reservists-Economic Party kept its four seats and remained above the electoral threshold. Meanwhile, the People of Israel party fell below the electoral threshold after receiving four seats in the previous poll.
A pollster for The Madad and Channel 13 News spoke with 103FM about the latest Channel 13 poll, explaining how the results of the two parties could affect the distribution of Knesset seats between the blocs.
Addressing a scenario in which one or both parties fail to cross the electoral threshold, he explained which bloc could benefit from the redistribution of seats.
"In terms of the balance between the blocs, if neither crosses the threshold, eight seats can be redistributed among other parties. However, one scenario is that one fails to cross the threshold and the other does, leaving four seats to be redistributed. Which party fails to cross the threshold could be significant. The side that would benefit more would be what we call the 'change bloc,' rather than the coalition bloc," he said, adding, "That is the conclusion we reached."
He also addressed where the two parties draw their support from and the differences between voters backing Winter and those supporting Hendel and Zelekha.
"People of Israel and the Reservists receive votes from both sides in almost equal measure. The question is when we start counting, whether we use the 2022 election as our starting point and ask where those votes were in the previous election," he explained.
"It is true that Hendel and Zelekha's votes come more evenly from both sides, while most of Winter's votes come from the coalition side. Nevertheless, Winter also took roughly one seat, out of the nearly four he has, from the opposition side, mainly from Liberman's party," he added.

articles.title_orig: Criminals who skip sentencing will face solitary confinement or lose social visits
articles.title_zh: Criminals who skip sentencing will face solitary confinement or lose social visits
articles.content_orig:
Judges in England and Wales will be given stronger powers to block prison visits and keep offenders in their cells for weeks on end if they refuse to face their victims' families during sentencing.
The tougher sanctions, due to come into effect next year, build on an existing law that orders criminals to attend sentencing or face being fined or jailed for another two years for contempt of court.
The move is the latest bid to push killers to attend court, with the Ministry of Justice acknowledging that longer jail time alone is unlikely to deter those already behind bars.
"Criminals should not be able to pick and choose when they face justice," Prisons Minister Catherine McKinnell said.
"Refusing to turn up to sentencing is an insult to victims and their families, and offenders must face the consequences," she added.
The new measures mean offenders could be confined to cells for up to three weeks, social visits could be banned for nearly a month and any prison privileges revoked for longer.
Farah Naz, the aunt of Zara Aleena who was sexually assaulted and murdered as she was walking home in Ilford, east London, in June 2022, said her niece's murderer refusing to come to court for sentencing "left a sense that justice was not quite complete".
She said Zara's family had hoped that by reading their victim impact statement in front of her murderer Jordan McSweeney, he would see "the consequence of his actions, of what he'd done, the devastation that he had caused". McSweeney was jailed for at least 38 years.
"Taking away these privileges... would rebalance the power in the justice system from offender to victim," Naz said.
Judges will also be able to restrict social visits further to once every four weeks for almost three months for criminals who refuse to attend sentencing.
For criminals aged 18-20, similar restrictions could be handed down, but for shorter periods of time, the Ministry of Justice said.
However, visits from prisoners' children will be exempt from the new sanctions.
But Pia Sinha, the CEO of Prison Reform Trust, has called for evidence that sanctions will increase attendance and warned the measures will punish relatives of prisoners who "have committed no offence themselves".
The families of murdered primary school teacher Sabina Nessa, law graduate Zara Aleena and mother-of-three Jan Mustafa have previously advocated for changes to the laws.
All of their loved ones' killers did not attend their sentencing hearings.
Thomas Cashman, the gunman who murdered nine-year-old Olivia Pratt-Korbel, and triple crossbow and knife killer Kyle Clifford, also refused to face their punishment in court.
Victims' Commissioner for England and Wales, Claire Waxman OBE, said the announcement follows "tireless efforts of victims' families" not accepting offenders simply "opting out of facing justice".
She said it was "essential" the powers were used "consistently by courts and prisons, so families receive the justice and accountability they deserve".

articles.title_zh: US orders some diplomats to leave Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks escalate
articles.content_orig:
The US State Department has ordered some diplomats and their families to leave Saudi Arabia as attacks escalate, with three people killed in strikes across the country.
Saudi authorities said debris from a drone intercepted during an attempted attack on an oil field killed two people, while one person died after a strike at the King Fahd International Airport in Dammam.
Conflict between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia has been rising in the past month.
The Houthis have responded to Saudi strikes by launching missiles and drones at airports, energy facilities and military bases in Saudi Arabia. A recent strike on Riyadh's international airport was the deadliest in the kingdom in years.
"The US Department of State issued an ordered departure for non-emergency US government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia," a state department spokesperson said in a statement.
"Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions," it added.
The spokesperson also warned "the hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly".
In the latest attack on the King Fahd International Airport eight people sustained injuries that ranged from "minor to serious", officials said.
No details of the attack have yet been given, but the strike comes after airports in Saudi Arabia have been repeatedly targeted by Houthi forces.
The energy ministry has also not said who had launched the drone aimed at the Shaybah oil field near the border with the United Arab Emirates that left two people injured.
Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa, in 2014. Conflicts escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led military coalition tried to restore the government's rule.
An informal ceasefire had been in place for the past four years, but it unravelled in July after the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they have called a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.
The group's "maritime embargo" in the Bab al-Mandab Strait along Yemen's south-western coast has contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.

articles.title_orig: Heidi Levine recounts how Palestinian youths helped save her in settler attack
articles.title_zh: Heidi Levine recounts how Palestinian youths helped save her in settler attack
articles.content_orig:
US photojournalist describes ‘protective shield’, vows to return to work in West Bank and criticises Netanyahu comments on incident
The Washington Post photojournalist who was attacked and seriously injured by Israeli settlers in the West Bank on Friday has described how she was saved with the help of local Palestinians.
Heidi Levine sustained four fractured vertebrae, two broken ribs and four puncture wounds when she was knocked to the ground and repeatedly beaten by a crowd of masked settlers while she and other journalists were covering the olive harvest in the Palestinian village of Abu Falah, north of Ramallah.
It is unclear whether the puncture wounds were caused by knives or other weapons. Levine said a witness to her attack had seen nails sticking out of some of the wooden clubs wielded by her attackers.
Levine, 64, has covered multiple wars and had just returned from an assignment in Ukraine before Friday’s attack. She said she would most likely have been killed had she not been wearing protective body armour and a helmet.
“I probably would have been dead, because for sure it doesn’t take much to kill a person with blows to the head,” she said shortly before being discharged from hospital on Wednesday in the Israeli city of Petah Tikva.
Levine pointed out that Palestinians did not have such protection and more than 20 had been killed in settler attacks so far this year, in the course of an escalating campaign of aggression – described as terrorism by Israeli security leaders – across the West Bank, aimed at driving Palestinians from their land.
“Every single journalist who looked at [the attack on me] are thinking they and I have gone to so many funerals of Palestinians killed by settlers,” Levine said.
She said the olive harvesting at Abu Falah had begun peacefully but at some point a group of young masked settlers appeared on a nearby hilltop watching the group of Palestinian villagers, journalists and human rights activists accompanying them. Levine said the attack began only after the Israeli army arrived on the scene.
“Then all hell broke loose. Some of the farmers started to gather their tarps and bags of olives that they had picked,” she said. “Then all of a sudden I hear a machine gun, and then saw teargas in the distance. I started to run … It was just like a lot of commotion and then all of a sudden I see a dozen of them and they started charging at me.
“I managed to keep my face to the ground, and I don’t know if I took that position to protect myself with my face down or it was their initial blow. Otherwise my whole face would have been broken and I could have suffered brain damage or lost an eye.
“They started kicking me and beating me with sticks. I can’t even count how many times, probably more than a hundred times. I actually tried playing dead so that they would stop. But it didn’t work.”
Witnesses said the beating only ceased when young Palestinian men used slingshots to aim stones at settlers forcing them back, allowing another American journalist, Jasper Nathaniel, to reach Levine and, with other reporters, help her to safety.
“The shabab [Palestinian youth] put themselves in front and were trying to keep them [the settlers] away, keep a protective shield, which was amazing. It was like a biblical battle,” Levine said.
After the attack, Nathaniel wrote : “Had the shabab not stepped up to protect her, she might well be dead. It is no exaggeration to say that young Palestinians armed only with stones risked their lives to save Heidi Levine’s.”
He said the army pursued the young Palestinians after the incident, rather than the settlers. Palestinians risk being shot by settlers or soldiers if they try to resist attacks, and can face long periods in detention without charge.
Levine, who has lived in Israel for four decades, said she would go back to reporting on the West Bank as soon as she recovered. “My work is important,” she said. “They have bruised me, broken some bones, but they haven’t cracked my spirit.”
Since the attack, she has received letters from Israelis expressing regret, and an apologetic phone call from the president, Isaac Herzog.
“He was a teddy bear on the phone,” she said. “He kept saying I just want to give you a big hug and these are not representative of who this country is, they’re a dark stain, and he called them thugs.”
The office of the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, however, put out a statement on X seeking to cast doubt on witness and video accounts of what he called an “alleged attack”.
Levine was particularly angered by Netanyahu’s claim that some video footage “appears to show Levine knocked down and immediately helped to her feet by the same unidentified individual”.
“That’s such bullshit. They helped me up because they couldn’t get my things off of me. That’s why,” Levine said. “They robbed me of everything I have – a pouch with my documents, my American passport, credit card, camera disk and a small camera bag with two other lenses. Everything is gone … That’s why [they stood me up], and then they threw me back down and continued to kick and hit me.”
The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, called the attack a “despicable act of terror” and demanded prosecutions. Israeli police arrested 10 suspects after the Abu Falah incident and another attack on Saturday aimed at European diplomats near the West Bank village of Taybeh.
On Wednesday an Israeli court released four suspects in the attack on Levine and put them under house arrest, on the grounds there was insufficient evidence to keep them in custody.
Asked if she expected her attackers to be brought to justice, Levine said her level of confidence was “two out of 10”.
“I am not very hopeful,” she said. “Of course, if the government made the decision to do something and crack down on this and get people arrested, they would do it. But it’s not just arresting these teenage thugs. It’s going after their leaders, the rabbis, and how they’re organised.”

AI companies for years have promised that smarter models would be worth the staggering cost to build them. Anthropic on Wednesday made that case in cash.

Yes, but: The company's blistering pace of growth appeared to slow compared with the difference between the first and second quarters, when sales more than doubled.

Flashback: Anthropic's early bets on coding expertise, business customers and spending discipline have paid off.
Reality check: Anthropic hasn't solved every financial challenge associated with the AI buildout.
What we're watching: Whether Anthropic can sustain its technological and financial advantages as it expands its frontier intelligence offerings into additional niche areas beyond coding.
The bottom line: Anthropic is showing Wall Street how frontier intelligence can turn into an actual business right when investors needed some good news.

articles.title_orig: Meta Ordered to Pay $25 Billion Over Cambridge Analytica Privacy Violations
articles.title_zh: Meta Ordered to Pay $25 Billion Over Cambridge Analytica Privacy Violations
articles.content_orig:
Meta was ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties by a New Mexico court on Wednesday as part of a data privacy case that stemmed from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal from nearly a decade ago.
The penalty, revealed in a court filing, comes after a jury in a Santa Fe courthouse found in September the social media giant liable for misleading state citizens about how it safeguards and collects user data and prevents harmful information from flourishing on its services.
Although the jury concluded that Meta had more than 43 million violations of the state's unfair practices act, with each transgression carrying a civil penalty as high as $5,000, a New Mexico judge was responsible for determining the ultimate fine. The Wednesday filing showed that the state was awarded $219.5 billion, but the penalty was ultimately reduced to $25 billion.
"The extraordinary number of willful violations found by the jury, the duration and repetition of the conduct, the breadth of subjects on which violations occurred, the involvement of senior Facebook leadership, the size of New Mexico audiences reached, and the clear intentional and systematic nature of Facebook's repeated misstatements established in the trial record support the highest level of penalty allowed by the New Mexico Unfair Practices Act - $5,000 per violation found by the jury," New Mexico District Court Judge Francis Mathew wrote in the filing.
The judge added that interest on the penalty shall accrue at the rate of 15% each year until the fine is paid off in full.
"For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law," said New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez in a statement.
He added that "this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences."
Meta chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney criticized the penalty, saying in a statement that the company is "confident" that it will "prevail on appeal."
"This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico," Mahoney said in the statement. "At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online."
Meta previously resolved various Cambridge Analytica-derived data privacy lawsuits across the nation as part of an overarching August settlement of nearly $17 billion with a coalition of state attorneys general in a separate federal case related to child safety and mental health. But because New Mexico was not part of the settlement, the state's data privacy case that arose from Meta's Cambridge Analytica scandal proceeded to trial in September.
In 2022, the social media giant agreed to pay $725 million to settle a class action lawsuit that also sprang from the company's Cambridge Analytica scandal that kicked off in 2018. That scandal rocked the Mark Zuckerberg -led company before its official name change to Meta, and focused on allegations that the political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica improperly accessed the information of 87 million users , raising questions about Facebook's data handling practices.
Mathew said in the filing that "Facebook did not conduct the comprehensive investigation that it promised" following the Cambridge Analytica revelations.
"Pressure from senior executives to keep costs down, lack of adequate enforcement resources, inadequate investigative techniques, and a desire not to create precedent for future investigations," all contributed to what the judge characterized as a "willfully ineffective" internal examination by Facebook, the filing said.
Former New Mexico Attorney General Hector Balderas originally filed the state's Cambridge Analytica-related lawsuit in 2021, while current AG Torrez oversaw the related trial.
Torrez also led his state's child safety-related trial against Meta that resulted in a March jury ruling that the social media company should pay $375 million for violating the state's unfair practices act. A New Mexico judge would later order Meta to pay $567 million into an abatement fund as part of a second phase of the case that determined the social media firm's actions created a public nuisance.
Meta said it disagreed with that New Mexico ruling and planned to appeal.
